name: Polyurethane (PUR): The Polymer That Dreams Are Made Of
notation_note: The structure shown pairs MDI with 1,4-butanediol, one diisocyanate-diol combination of very many. Polyurethane is a linkage rather than a single chemistry: the same urethane group joins whatever diol and diisocyanate a formulation calls for, which is how one family spans soft foam to rigid insulation to elastomer.
era: The Birth of Synthetic Polymers (1907-1938): The Bakelite Revolution
historical_events_referenced: Death of Wallace Carothers, DuPont's chief chemist and inventor of nylon (29 April 1937)
Otto Bayer's diisocyanate polyaddition patent published (November 1937)

historical_images.alt: A man in round wire-rimmed glasses and a suit, in a laboratory, holding up a translucent strip of material and examining it, with glassware visible behind him.
historical_images.caption: Wallace Carothers in his DuPont laboratory. His patents on polyester and polyamide fibers were so comprehensive that a rival chemistry, not a rival patent fight, was the only way around them.
historical_images.author: Unknown photographer

historical_images.alt: A smiling man in a suit stands over laboratory glassware from which a large mass of pale, irregularly bulging foam has risen and overflowed a beaker.
historical_images.caption: Otto Bayer in 1952, demonstrating the reaction he had patented fifteen years earlier: mix an isocyanate with a polyol, and the beaker fills itself.
historical_images.author: Bayer AG

historical_images.alt: A hand pressing into a pale, off-white block of foam, which shows only a shallow, fading impression around the fingers as it springs back.
historical_images.caption: Conventional flexible polyurethane foam recovers its shape within seconds of a hand lifting away.
historical_images.author: Johan

historical_images.alt: A hand hovering just above a bright yellow block of foam that retains a deep, detailed impression of fingers and palm after the hand has lifted away.
historical_images.caption: Viscoelastic 'memory' polyurethane foam holds the same impression far longer — the slow recovery that gives the material its name.
historical_images.author: Johan

density.conditions: solid/cast form, general (Wypych); a fully crystalline PU is calculated at 1.322 g/cm³, and an MDI/1,4-butanediol system is measured at 1.297 g/cm³ (Mark)

melt_flow_index.conditions: Formed by reactive polyaddition/casting, not conventional melt processing, for most grades.

electrical_conductivity.conditions: reciprocal of reported volume resistivity, 4.8×10⁹ Ω·m, solid/cast form

water_absorption.conditions: water vapor absorption, MDI/ethylene glycol system

synthesis.industrial_process_notes: Otto Bayer and coworkers at IG Farben (Leverkusen) first made polyurethanes in 1937. Commercial polyisocyanates became available in 1952 and flexible foam production began in 1954. Industrially formed by mixing an isocyanate ('A-side') with a polyol blend containing catalysts and additives ('B-side'), then dispensing into molds/substrates to cure. Foams account for ~67% of all polyurethane produced (2016 data); ~25 million tonnes produced globally in 2019.

structure_morphology.crystal_structure: Triclinic unit cell most commonly reported for hard-segment crystallites (e.g. MDI/1,4-butanediol); polymorphs I and II form under quiescent crystallization, polymorph III under orientation/strain.
structure_morphology.chain_flexibility_notes: Rigid foams use high crosslink density (thermal insulation); flexible foams use longer chain segments with lower crosslinking; elastomers sit at an intermediate crosslink density.

a.conditions: MDI/1,4-butanediol system; an exponent this high suggests chain association/aggregation in solution rather than simple coil expansion

tg.conditions: solid/cast form, general; Mark reports much higher hard-segment Tg values for specific systems, e.g. -2 to 90 °C across HMDI/BD, HMDI/DEG, and MDI/EG

tm.conditions: DSC, solid/cast form, general; Mark reports 123-225 °C across specific systems (HMDI/DEG, HMDI/OFHD, TDI/EG, MDI/EG)

decomposition_onset.conditions: as reported; unusually low for typical PU thermal decomposition (commonly cited around 250-300 °C), possibly reflecting a specific low-stability formulation

thermal_conductivity.conditions: Rigid PUR foam is a well-known low-thermal-conductivity insulation material; the only handbook figure found (0.13 W/(m·K)) is explicitly for the melt state, not solid, so is not recorded here.

yield_strength.conditions: tensile stress at yield, solid/cast form

hardness.conditions: solid/cast form; harder grades reported separately as Shore D 36-91

hydrolysis_resistance.conditions: Ester-based PUR is known to be more hydrolysis-prone than ether-based PUR -- a real, widely-cited distinction, but not independently confirmed with a source.

solubility_parameter.conditions: Hildebrand parameter, solid/cast form, general; Mark reports 21-27 MPa^0.5 across specific MDI/1,4-butanediol and MDI/ethylene glycol systems

environmental.environmental_notes: As a broad, highly formulation-dependent thermoset/elastomer family, end-of-life handling varies widely by product type; chemical recycling (e.g. glycolysis) exists for some grades but is not yet mainstream.
